{{Short description|Way of decomposing a topological space}}
In [[topology]], a branch of mathematics, an '''abstract [[stratified space]]''', or a '''Thom–Mather stratified space''' is a [[topological space]] ''X'' that has been decomposed into pieces called '''strata'''; these strata are [[manifold]]s and are required to fit together in a certain way. Thom–Mather stratified spaces provide a purely topological setting{{Clarify |  How is it purely topological? In the definition below each stratum is required to be a smooth manifold, making it not a purely topological construction?|date=May 2026}} for the study of singularities analogous to the more differential-geometric theory of [[Hassler Whitney|Whitney]].  They were introduced in 1969 by [[René Thom]], who showed that every [[Whitney conditions |Whitney stratified space]] was also a topologically stratified space, with the same strata. Another proof was given by [[John Mather (mathematician)|John Mather]] in 1970, inspired by Thom's proof.

Basic examples of Thom–Mather stratified spaces include [[manifolds with boundary]] (top dimension and codimension 1 boundary) and [[manifold with corners|manifolds with corners]] (top dimension, codimension 1 boundary, codimension 2 corners), real or complex analytic varieties, or orbit spaces of smooth transformation groups.

==Definition==

A Thom–Mather stratified space is a triple <math>(V, {\mathcal S}, {\mathfrak J})</math> where <math>V</math> is a topological space (often we require that it is [[locally compact]], [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], and [[second countable]]), <math>{\mathcal S}</math> is a decomposition of <math>V</math> into '''strata,'''

:<math> V = \bigsqcup_{X\in {\mathcal S}} X, </math>

and <math>{\mathfrak J}</math> is the set of '''control data''' <math>\{ (T_X), (\pi_X), (\rho_X)\ | X\in S\}</math> where <math>T_X</math> is an open neighborhood of the stratum <math>X</math> (called the tubular neighborhood), <math>\pi_X: T_X \to X</math> is a continuous retraction, and <math>\rho_X: T_X \to [0, +\infty)</math> is a continuous function. These data need to satisfy the following conditions. 

# Each stratum <math>X</math> is a [[locally closed subset]] and the decomposition <math>S</math> is [[Locally finite collection|locally finite]].
# The decomposition <math>S</math> satisfies the axiom of the frontier: if <math>X, Y \in {\mathcal S}</math> and <math> Y \cap \overline{X} \neq \emptyset</math>, then <math>Y \subseteq \overline{X}</math>. This condition implies that there is a [[partial order]] among strata: <math>Y<X</math> if and only if <math>Y \subset\overline{X}</math> and <math>Y \neq X</math>.
# Each stratum <math>X</math> is a smooth manifold.
# <math>X = \{ v \in T_X\ |\ \rho_X(v) = 0\}</math>. So <math>\rho_X</math> can be viewed as the ''distance function'' from the stratum <math>X</math>.
# For each pair of strata <math>Y<X</math>, the restriction <math>(\pi_Y, \rho_Y): T_Y \cap X \to Y \times (0, +\infty)</math> is a [[submersion (mathematics)|submersion]].
# For each pair of strata <math>Y<X</math>, there holds <math>\pi_Y \circ \pi_X = \pi_Y</math> and <math>\rho_Y \circ \pi_X = \rho_Y</math> (both over the common domain of both sides of the equation).

== Examples ==
One of the original motivations for stratified spaces were decomposing singular spaces into smooth chunks. For example, given a singular variety <math>X</math>, there is a naturally defined subvariety, <math>\mathrm{Sing}(X)</math>, which is the singular locus. This may not be a smooth variety, so taking the iterated singularity locus <math>\mathrm{Sing}(\mathrm{Sing}(X))</math> will eventually give a natural stratification.{{fact|date=July 2022}} A simple algebreo-geometric example is the singular [[hypersurface]]

{{in5}}<math>\text{Spec}\left(\Complex[x,y,z]/\left(x^4 + y^4 + z^4\right)\right) \xleftarrow{(0,0,0)} \text{Spec}(\Complex)</math>

where <math>\text{Spec}(-)</math> is the [[Spectrum of a ring|prime spectrum]].
